opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the things that keeps me up at night with this whole research direction. The basic idea is appealing: you train a model only on text up to some cutoff, say 1930, and then ask it to forecast what happens next. Because we know what actually happened, you get a clean backtest of forecasting ability, which you can't get with a model trained on today's internet, where you'd have to wait years to find out whether it was right.

But the "only on text up to the cutoff" part is much harder than it sounds. The most obvious problem is dating. A huge fraction of historical documents don't have reliable dates attached, or the dates in the metadata are when something was digitized or republished, not written. So you get a 1960s reprint of an 1890s book with a new introduction that mentions the World Wars, and it slips into your pre-1900 corpus.

Then there's subtler stuff. Editorial choices are a form of leakage. Which documents survived, which got digitized, which got transcribed carefully: those choices were made by people who knew how history turned out. Things that seemed important in hindsight are overrepresented. So even if every token is genuinely pre-cutoff, the distribution of what the model sees is shaped by the future. A model might "predict" that some obscure political movement will matter just because its writings are suspiciously well preserved.

There's also leakage through the pipeline itself: tokenizers built on modern text, OCR correction models trained on modern language, filtering classifiers, and especially any fine-tuning or instruction tuning. If you use a modern model to clean up or label your historical data, you're injecting knowledge of the future. And if you want the model to be a useful chat assistant, the cheapest way is to tune it on modern instruction data, which is a disaster for this purpose.

And finally, the evaluation side leaks. Researchers choose which questions to ask, and we're naturally drawn to events we know turned out to be important. That isn't the model cheating, but it can make forecasting look better or worse than it really is.

So my view is that you need to be really paranoid: build classifiers to detect anachronisms, check for things like modern spellings or references, hold out data and look for suspicious knowledge, and frankly accept that you'll never get it perfectly clean. The question is whether you can get it clean enough that the remaining leakage is small relative to the signal you're trying to measure. I think it's worth trying, but I'd be skeptical of any striking results until people have really hammered on the contamination question.

r001.rationale: The response mentions anachronism classifiers, modern spellings, and references, but does not identify LLMs’ knowledge of when language was used as a detection method.

r002.rationale: It says researchers are drawn to questions about events known to have turned out important, making question selection itself a source of leakage.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because it's one of those problems that looks like a technicality but actually undermines the whole enterprise if you're not careful.

The basic setup people want is: take a model, train it only on text up to some cutoff date, then ask it to predict what happened after that. If it does well, great, you've got evidence that the model can genuinely forecast rather than just recall. The trouble is that "trained only on text up to date X" is a much harder guarantee to make than it sounds.

The first issue is just that dates on documents are unreliable. Wikipedia articles get edited continuously, so an article about some 2019 event might contain sentences written in 2023 that explain how it all turned out. Forum posts get quoted in later threads. News archives get updated with corrections and follow-ups. So even if you filter by the nominal publication date, you're letting in a lot of hindsight.

The second, subtler issue is that information about the future leaks in through text that doesn't explicitly mention the future. If you train on documents up to 2020, but your training set was assembled in 2024, the selection of which documents survived and got scraped is itself shaped by what happened afterward. The things that turned out to matter got linked to more, archived more, discussed more. So the distribution of your "historical" corpus already encodes outcomes, even if no individual document does.

And then there's a third thing I find really hard to rule out, which is that the model may have been exposed to data at other stages. Pre-training is one thing, but then there's instruction tuning, RLHF, whatever evaluation data got folded in. If any of that is more recent, you've contaminated the forecast. And frankly, with the big labs' models, you usually can't audit this at all. You're just taking their word for it.

So when I see a paper claiming a model achieved some impressive forecasting accuracy on events after its cutoff, my first reaction is skepticism, not because I think the authors are being sloppy, but because I think the clean experiment is close to impossible to run with existing models. The honest version is probably to train your own model from scratch on a carefully curated snapshot, which almost nobody has the resources to do, or to only forecast events that happen after the model was actually deployed, which means you have to wait around for reality to catch up.

That second approach is actually what I'd push people toward. It's slow, but it's the only version where you can be confident the model didn't peek.

r001.rationale: The response discusses unreliable document dates and later edits, but does not identify an LLM’s knowledge of when language was used as a way to detect anachronistic contamination.

r002.rationale: The response says that later outcomes can shape which historical documents survive or get scraped. It does not explain that choosing forecasting questions based on events known to have occurred later can leak future information.

astra-6.text:
Well, the worry is that you think you’re testing forecasting ability, but you’re actually testing whether the model remembers what happened. If you ask it to make a prediction as of 2015, but it was trained on text from 2020, telling it to pretend it’s 2015 doesn’t remove that information.

And the leakage can be quite subtle. You could remove every explicit mention of the outcome, but later text will still reflect it—in which people get discussed, which companies are considered important, or which ideas are treated as promising. So I wouldn’t be very confident that you could clean a later training set sufficiently to make that historical test convincing.

What I’d find much more persuasive is to fix the model, have it make predictions about events that haven’t happened yet, and then wait. That’s slower, unfortunately, but it gives you a much clearer answer about whether it can actually forecast.

r001.rationale: The response describes later training data leaking outcomes through explicit and subtle content, but does not identify the model’s knowledge of when language was used as a way to detect anachronistic contamination.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that choosing historical forecasting questions based on events later known to have occurred can itself leak future information.

sol-6.1.text:
The main concern is that it’s very hard to tell whether you’re measuring forecasting ability or the model remembering what happened. If you ask it to make a prediction as of 2015, saying “Pretend you don’t know anything after 2015” doesn’t actually remove that information from its weights.

And the leakage can be quite subtle. You might remove an article that reports the outcome, but leave in later text that refers to the people or organisations involved in a way that gives it away. Even which questions you choose can leak information: we tend to ask about events because they subsequently became important.

So I’d be much more convinced by prospective evaluations: record the model’s predictions before the outcomes occur, and then score them afterwards. Historical evaluations can still be useful, but you need a model whose training data genuinely stops before the prediction date, and a lot of care about how you select the questions. Otherwise, an impressive result can be very difficult to interpret.
